blocks.text: 1. Seasonality

blocks.alt: A pattern that repeats at a fixed interval is seasonality

blocks.text: Trend, the previous topic, covered the first of the two common causes of non-stationarity already previewed in the Stationarity topic: a sustained, long-term directional movement in a series. Seasonality covers the second: a repeating, predictable pattern that recurs at fixed, known intervals, a genuinely different kind of structure from trend's steady, sustained directional movement.

This directly connects back to a specific, concrete caveat already raised for Time Series Split in the Cross Validation module: different rounds of that walk-forward validation split could land on genuinely different parts of the exact same seasonal cycle, one round's test period falling entirely within a holiday spike, another falling entirely within an ordinary, quiet period, purely as a consequence of chronological timing. This topic explains exactly why that caveat mattered so much.
2. The Definition

Seasonality refers to a pattern that repeats at fixed, known, predictable intervals throughout a time series. Retail sales spiking every single December, year after year, is a classic, immediately recognizable example. Website traffic consistently dipping every single weekend, week after week, is another.

The defining trait separating genuine seasonality from other kinds of repeating structure is that the interval between repetitions is fixed and known in advance, once a year for the December sales spike, once a week for the weekend traffic dip, rather than occurring at irregular, unpredictable intervals. This fixed, predictable timing is exactly what makes seasonality something that can be systematically identified, quantified, and explicitly modeled, covered throughout the rest of this topic.
3. Seasonality versus Trend

blocks.alt: Seasonality repeats on a fixed cycle while trend moves in one long direction

blocks.text: It is worth drawing the contrast with trend, covered in the previous topic, directly. Trend is a sustained, long-term directional movement, values consistently climbing or consistently falling over the overall span of the series. Seasonality is instead a repeating, cyclical pattern, values rising and falling in a consistent, predictable rhythm that repeats over and over throughout the series.

A real time series can have neither of these components, either one alone, or genuinely both simultaneously, and recognizing which components are actually present matters directly for choosing the right modeling approach. Retail sales offer a clean example of both operating together: a genuine rising trend from one year to the next, reflecting overall business growth, combined with a repeating December spike that shows up every single year regardless of that underlying year-over-year growth trend.
4. The Seasonal Period

blocks.alt: A series has a seasonal period, like every 12 months

blocks.text: The seasonal period is the fixed length of one complete repeating cycle, and correctly identifying it is the essential first step before modeling seasonality at all. Daily data showing a weekly repeating pattern has a seasonal period of 7, since the pattern completes one full cycle every 7 daily observations.

Monthly data showing a yearly repeating pattern has a seasonal period of 12, one full cycle every 12 monthly observations. Hourly data showing a daily repeating pattern has a seasonal period of 24, one full cycle every 24 hourly observations. Getting this period exactly right matters directly for every technique covered in the rest of this topic, since seasonal differencing, autocorrelation-based detection, and explicit seasonal modeling all depend on knowing the correct period to actually work with.
5. Seasonal Differencing

blocks.alt: A value minus the value from one full period back removes seasonality

blocks.text: This connects directly back to ordinary differencing, already covered in depth in the Stationarity topic, which subtracts each value from the value immediately preceding it. Seasonal differencing works differently: rather than subtracting the immediately preceding value, it subtracts the value from exactly one full seasonal period earlier, the correct period identified using the guidance covered in the previous section.

For monthly data with a yearly seasonal pattern, seasonal differencing subtracts each month's value from that same month's value one full year, 12 months, earlier, rather than from the immediately preceding month. This directly removes the repeating seasonal pattern from the series, moving it considerably closer to stationary, exactly the property covered in depth in the Stationarity topic, and it is often used together with ordinary differencing when a series has both a trend and a seasonal pattern present simultaneously.
6. Directly Explaining Time Series Split's Caveat

It is worth returning directly to the specific caveat already raised for Time Series Split in the Cross Validation module, since understanding seasonality thoroughly, as covered throughout this topic, directly explains exactly why that caveat mattered so much. An early round of a walk-forward validation split could have its test period land entirely within a low-activity season, while a later round's test period lands entirely within a high-activity season, purely as a consequence of when each round's test period happens to fall within the overall seasonal cycle.

This means a model's reported performance can look wildly different from one round to the next, not because the model itself is genuinely inconsistent, but purely because different rounds happened to test on genuinely different, non-comparable parts of the same underlying seasonal cycle. Recognizing this directly is exactly why that earlier topic recommended checking that test periods span a reasonably representative mix of whatever seasonal variation actually exists in the data.

blocks.text: 7. Detecting Seasonality

blocks.alt: A series runs through an autocorrelation plot to detect seasonality

blocks.text: The simplest first check for seasonality is visual: plot the series and look for a pattern that repeats at a consistent, recognizable interval, exactly the same kind of visual inspection already covered as a first check for stationarity in an earlier topic. A more rigorous, formal check uses autocorrelation, which measures how strongly a series correlates with a lagged, shifted version of itself, at various different lag values.

A strong, clearly visible spike in autocorrelation appearing at exactly the suspected seasonal period, lag 12 for a suspected yearly pattern in monthly data, for instance, confirms genuine, statistically meaningful seasonality at that specific period, rather than just a visually suggestive but ultimately coincidental pattern. This autocorrelation-based check is the standard, formal way to confirm both that seasonality genuinely exists in a series and exactly what its correct period actually is.
8. Multiple Seasonalities

blocks.alt: A series can have a daily seasonality and a yearly seasonality at once

blocks.text: Some real time series genuinely have more than one seasonal pattern operating simultaneously, a situation worth being aware of directly. Hourly electricity demand offers a classic, concrete example: a daily cycle, reflecting higher demand during waking hours and lower demand overnight, a weekly cycle, reflecting different demand patterns on weekdays versus weekends, and a yearly cycle, reflecting seasonal temperature-driven demand for heating or cooling, can all operate at once within the exact same series.

Each of these distinct cycles needs to be identified and modeled in its own right, using the detection and differencing techniques already covered throughout this topic, applied separately at each relevant seasonal period. This is a genuinely more complex modeling situation than a series with just a single seasonal pattern, but it is a real, common occurrence in practice, particularly for high-frequency data like hourly or sub-hourly measurements.

blocks.text: 9. Seasonality as a Feature

blocks.alt: Seasonality is covered here, lag features come next

blocks.text: It is worth previewing a connection directly to the Feature Engineering topic, covered later in this module, mirroring the exact same connection already made for trend as a feature in the previous topic. Rather than only using seasonal information to achieve stationarity through seasonal differencing, already covered earlier in this topic, seasonal information can itself be directly encoded as input features for a machine learning model.

Encoding the month, the day of the week, or the hour of the day directly as features lets a machine learning model learn seasonal patterns directly from the data itself, alongside every other feature it uses, rather than requiring seasonality to be explicitly removed through differencing before modeling can even begin. This turns seasonality, exactly like trend before it, from a purely statistical preprocessing concern into a genuinely useful piece of information a model can directly learn from and exploit.
10. Worked Example
The example below detects a yearly seasonal pattern in monthly data using autocorrelation, then applies seasonal differencing and confirms the result moves closer to stationary.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, acf

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
n_years = 8
months_per_year = 12
n_points = n_years * months_per_year

# Monthly data with a clear yearly seasonal pattern (higher in December, month index 11)
time_index = np.arange(n_points)
seasonal_pattern = 10 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time_index / months_per_year - np.pi / 2)
series = 50 + seasonal_pattern + rng.normal(scale=2, size=n_points)

# Check autocorrelation at various lags
autocorrelations = acf(series, nlags=13)
print("Autocorrelation at lag 12 (yearly, for monthly data):", round(autocorrelations[12], 3))
print("Autocorrelation at lag 6 (half-year, for comparison):", round(autocorrelations[6], 3))

# Seasonal differencing: subtract the value from exactly one year (12 months) earlier
seasonally_differenced = series[months_per_year:] - series[:-months_per_year]

for name, s in [("Original series", series), ("Seasonally differenced series", seasonally_differenced)]:
    p_value = adfuller(s)[1]
    print(f"{name}: ADF p-value = {p_value:.4f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The autocorrelation at lag 12 should be noticeably higher than at lag 6, confirming the genuine yearly seasonal pattern built into this example, and the seasonally differenced series should show a smaller ADF p-value, confirming the seasonal pattern has been successfully removed.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Seasonality is a pattern repeating at a fixed, known interval, distinct from trend's sustained, long-term direction.
A series can have neither trend nor seasonality, either one alone, or genuinely both simultaneously.
The seasonal period, the fixed length of one repeating cycle, must be correctly identified before modeling seasonality.
Seasonal differencing subtracts the value from exactly one full seasonal period earlier, removing the repeating pattern.
Understanding seasonality directly explains why different Time Series Split rounds can land on non-comparable parts of a cycle.
Autocorrelation formally confirms seasonality, with a spike at exactly the suspected seasonal period.
Some series, like hourly electricity demand, have multiple seasonal patterns operating simultaneously.
Seasonal information, like month or day of week, can itself become a feature fed directly into a model, previewing Feature Engineering.
Next up: Feature Engineering, covering how to turn a time series into machine-learning-ready features more broadly.
